patient.chief_complaint: 12-year history of 'visual zigzags' before severe headaches — now requesting better management after recent worsening
patient.hpi:
A 45-year-old Polish-British man presented to the neurology outpatient clinic for assessment and management optimisation of long-standing migraine with aura. He has experienced episodic visual aura followed by severe headache since age 33. His typical episode begins with a small, bright, jagged zigzag line appearing near the centre of his vision on one side that slowly moves outward and expands into a crescent-shaped arc of shimmering, flickering light over 20-30 minutes before disappearing from the periphery. The affected visual field feels 'blurry' while the aura is present. Within 10-15 minutes of the aura resolving, a severe unilateral throbbing headache develops (8-9/10 intensity), predominantly right-sided but occasionally left-sided, with marked nausea, occasional vomiting, intense photophobia and phonophobia. Attacks last 8-24 hours and leave him wiped out for the rest of the day.

Episodes were previously 1-2/month but have increased to 3-4/month over the past 6 months. He attributes this to a very stressful period at work — he was recently promoted and is now managing a team of 20 people with long hours and frequent travel. He also notes he sleeps poorly and has been drinking more coffee (4-5 cups/day). He uses rizatriptan 10 mg wafers as needed which are effective if taken early, but he delays taking them hoping the headache will be mild and runs out before month end, then uses codeine-paracetamol compound for remaining attacks.

He is a non-smoker, has mild hypertension managed with amlodipine, and has no cardiac disease. His father had similar headaches. He is not on preventive migraine therapy.
pmh: No cardiac disease, no TIA, no diabetes

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Established migraine with typical visual aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1) with medication-overuse risk from co-codamol

differential.key_features: Co-codamol use ≥10 days/month for ≥3 months meets ICHD-3 criteria for MOH; must be addressed [Holland_2012]
Headache days approaching ≥15/month over 3 months — quantify

optimal_actions.action: Search guideline literature to confirm ICHD-3 1.2 criteria for migraine with aura and exclude SNOOP/CHATS red flags
optimal_actions.expected_finding: ICHD-3 criteria for migraine with aura confirmed; no SNOOP red flag present that mandates further workup

tool_parameters.query: ICHD-3 migraine with aura diagnostic criteria SNOOP red flags

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions and contraindications for acute (triptan/ergotamine/CGRP antagonist) and prophylactic (beta-blocker, topiramate, valproate, amitriptyline) migraine medications appropriate to this patient
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Withdraw co-codamol (taper); initiate preventive therapy (topiramate or propranolol); rizatriptan as acute therapy ≤2 days/week [Holland_2012]

optimal_actions.action: Take a structured headache and aura history against ICHD-3 1.2: number of attacks, aura modality and full reversibility, gradual spread over at least five minutes, duration of each symptom between five and sixty minutes, unilaterality, temporal relation to the headache, and a documented red-flag review. This is the diagnostic test for this condition
optimal_actions.expected_finding: ICHD-3 1.2 criteria documented item by item against the reference set for this subtype, with the red-flag review recorded

useless_tools.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here
Routine transthoracic / bubble echocardiogram (PFO screening) is NOT indicated in migraine with aura; PFO-migraine association is controversial and PFO closure does not reduce migraine [Charles_2017]
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura — no role unless cardioembolic stroke is on the differential
EEG is not indicated for migraine with aura; reserve for cases where focal seizure is genuinely on the differential

critical_actions: Address medication-overuse headache — withdraw codeine-containing compound analgesic
Limit acute triptan use to ≤2 days/week to avoid MOH recurrence
contraindicated_actions: Do not continue compound codeine analgesics for migraine — they cause MOH and are not recommended for migraine [Holland_2012]
Do not co-administer ergotamines with triptans
key_reasoning_points: Compound opioid analgesics are inappropriate for migraine and a leading driver of medication-overuse headache
Long-standing untreated migraine with aura with current MOH risk warrants both withdrawal and preventive therapy [Holland_2012]

red_herrings.intended_effect: May appear to be a routine analgesic regimen
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Codeine compound analgesics are inappropriate for migraine and drive MOH; should be tapered off

red_herrings.data_point: Borderline hyperlipidaemia and mild hypertension suggesting cerebrovascular disease
red_herrings.intended_effect: A 45-year-old man with hypertension, borderline cholesterol, and WMH on MRI might prompt cerebrovascular workup
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: WMH are in non-specific subcortical pattern consistent with migraine; no periventricular lesions; no lacunar infarcts; DWI normal; the primary issues are medication overuse risk and unaddressed preventive therapy need

red_herrings.data_point: Increased attack frequency — possible transformation to chronic migraine
red_herrings.intended_effect: Escalation to 3-4 attacks/month over 6 months might suggest chronic migraine transformation
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Frequency escalation explained by identified modifiable factors: work stress, increased caffeine (4-5 cups/day), incipient codeine overuse, and absence of preventive therapy

clinical_assessment.impression: Structured headache and aura history taken against ICHD-3 1.2. 4 of the four criterion-C characteristics are documented — the diagnosis is met on the history, which is the only test that establishes it. The distinction from a transient ischaemic attack is made here and not by imaging: aura spreads gradually over minutes and is positive before it is negative, whereas ischaemia is abrupt and negative from the outset. Imaging is for the red flags this history screens for, not for the diagnosis.

output.summary:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Medication Overuse Headache (MOH) — Opioid/Codeine Risk KEY FINDINGS:
1. MOH DEFINITION: Headache on ≥15 days/month in a patient using acute headache medications ≥10 days/month (opioids) or ≥15 days/month (NSAIDs/acetaminophen) for >3 months
2. OPIOID/CODEINE: Highest risk for MOH — even 10 days/month can cause medication overuse; opioids increase central sensitisation
3. CURRENT PATIENT: Co-codamol 6-8 days/month IN ADDITION to rizatriptan 4/month = total ~10-12 treatment days/month — BORDERLINE/AT RISK
4. TRIPTAN OVERUSE: Triptans >10 days/month can cause triptan-overuse headache — but rizatriptan at 4/month is safe
5. MANAGEMENT: Withdraw overused medication; bridge with NSAIDs during washout; preventive therapy reduces need for acute medications
6. CAFFEINE: 4-5 cups/day is excessive; caffeine withdrawal itself triggers headache; daily caffeine >200 mg contributes to rebound headache CONCLUSION: Codeine overuse is a significant concern — 6-8 days/month of co-codamol is at threshold for MOH. Urgent need to withdraw codeine compounds and initiate preventive therapy. Opioid-containing analgesics used on ≥10 days per month carry the highest risk of medication overuse headache (MOH) among acute migraine treatments; withdrawal of overused opioid compounds is the primary intervention; preventive migraine therapy reduces the need for acute medication; daily caffeine above 200-400 mg/day is associated with increased migraine frequency and rebound headache risk

LITERATURE SEARCH: Migraine Prevention — Options in a 45-Year-Old Man with Hypertension KEY FINDINGS:
1. PROPRANOLOL 40-120 mg BID: First-line; dual benefit for hypertension AND migraine prevention; Level A evidence; AVOID if depression/asthma
2. AMLODIPINE (already prescribed): Calcium channel blockers have modest migraine prevention benefit; however, amlodipine has limited migraine-specific evidence vs verapamil
3. CANDESARTAN 16 mg/day: ARB with Level B evidence for migraine prevention; additional antihypertensive benefit; good option if beta-blocker not tolerated
4. TOPIRAMATE 50-100 mg/day: Level A; no teratogenicity concern in men; mild weight loss benefit; cognitive side effects
5. AMITRIPTYLINE 10-75 mg QHS: Level B; useful if poor sleep or comorbid anxiety
6. ANTI-CGRP ANTIBODIES: After failure of 2-3 first-line agents NOTE: Patient has mild hypertension on amlodipine — propranolol would be excellent dual-purpose preventive. Check for contraindications (asthma, depression, bradycardia). CONCLUSION: Add propranolol 40 mg BID (increasing to 80 mg BID) — dual benefit for migraine prevention and hypertension; may allow amlodipine dose reduction. Propranolol (Level A) has dual evidence for migraine prevention and hypertension management, making it a preferred first-line agent when both conditions coexist; topiramate (Level A) and candesartan (Level B) are established alternatives; preventive efficacy is best assessed after overused analgesics have been withdrawn, as MOH can blunt the response to preventive therapy

output.summary: DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW — RIZATRIPTAN + PROPRANOLOL Query: Adding propranolol preventive to patient already using rizatriptan FINDINGS: SIGNIFICANT INTERACTION: Propranolol inhibits CYP2D6 and P-glycoprotein transport of rizatriptan, increasing rizatriptan plasma concentration by ~67% CLINICAL CONSEQUENCE: Increased rizatriptan exposure can increase side effects (chest tightness, dizziness, fatigue) MANUFACTURER RECOMMENDATION: When co-administering propranolol and rizatriptan, REDUCE rizatriptan dose to 5 mg (not 10 mg); maximum 2 tablets/day ALTERNATIVE: If rizatriptan dose reduction is undesirable, use a triptan NOT affected by propranolol (e.g., sumatriptan 50-100 mg, eletriptan 40 mg) CONCLUSION: CLINICALLY SIGNIFICANT interaction — propranolol substantially increases rizatriptan systemic exposure via CYP2D6/P-gp inhibition; manufacturer labelling recommends dose reduction of rizatriptan when these agents are co-prescribed. Clinical management per prescriber assessment. Propranolol increases rizatriptan exposure ~67% via CYP2D6/P-gp inhibition; manufacturer labelling recommends rizatriptan dose reduction when co-prescribed

LITERATURE SEARCH: Caffeine and Migraine KEY FINDINGS:
1. DOSE-RESPONSE: >400 mg caffeine/day (approximately 4 cups brewed coffee) associated with increased migraine frequency; 1-2 cups/day may be safe for most migraineurs
2. WITHDRAWAL HEADACHE: Caffeine withdrawal headache is diffuse, throbbing, peaks at 20-51 hours after cessation; gradual taper recommended
3. REBOUND CYCLE: daily caffeine use can contribute to 'rebound' or 'transformed' migraine; intake of 4-5 cups/day carries this risk
4. REDUCTION STRATEGY: Reduce by 25% per week; switch some cups to tea or decaffeinated; avoid abrupt cessation CONCLUSION: Caffeine reduction from 4-5 cups/day to ≤2 cups/day is recommended — gradual taper over 3-4 weeks. Caffeine >400 mg/day increases migraine frequency; gradual reduction to ≤2 cups/day recommended; avoid abrupt cessation (withdrawal headache)
